extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and staging tragic drama: principles for moving pity and terror, staging effects, costume and spectacle, and what to avoid so the poetry (thought and expression) — not mechanical artifices — creates the emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid raising terror and pity by dresses and decorations
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary writers in tragedy endeavour to raise Terror and Pity ... by the Dresses and Decorations of the Stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues we should have our Conceptions raised by the Dignity of Thought and Sublimity of Expression, rather than by robes, feathers, or other stage trappings. Mechanical artifices may affect ordinary minds, but a good poet should rely on sentiment and language to inflame the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make greatness depend on costume (huge plumes and trains)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary Method of making an Hero, is to clap a huge Plume of Feathers upon his Head ... a Princess generally receives her Grandeur from those additional Incumbrances that fall into her Tail: I mean the broad sweeping Train that follows her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large feathers force actors into awkward stiffness and distract the audience (one's eye is taken up with the page tending the train). Costuming should not be the source of a character's dignity; it must not impede natural action or attention to speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell of great multitudes or battles rather than represent them on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible for the Reader's Imagination to multiply twenty Men into such prodigious Multitudes, or to fancy that two or three hundred thousand Soldiers are fighting in a Room of forty or fifty Yards in Compass. Incidents of such a Nature should be told, not represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attempting to represent vast armies or large-scale battles in a small theatre; such spectacle strains credulity and is better conveyed by description or reported action in the dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer unattended monarchs and avoid noisy martial effects (imitate French stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: I should therefore, in this Particular, recommend to my Countrymen the Example of the French Stage, where the Kings and Queens always appear unattended, and leave their Guards behind the Scenes. I should likewise be glad if we imitated the French in banishing from our Stage the Noise of Drums, Trumpets, and Huzzas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restraint in ostentation (no drum-and-trumpet fanfare or stage legions) produces a more polite, dignified theatre; noisy martial paraphernalia often becomes absurd (author cites battle noise heard to Charing-Cross).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thunder, lightning, bells, ghosts, etc., sparingly and skillfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the several Artifices ... the first Place is due to Thunder and Lightning ... There is something of this kind very ridiculous in the English Theatre. ... I have known a Bell introduced into several Tragedies with good Effect; and have seen the whole Assembly in a very great Alarm all the while it has been ringing. There is nothing which delights and terrifies our English Theatre so much as a Ghost, especially when he appears in a bloody Shirt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such stage effects can be powerful when introduced with skill, in proper season, and accompanied by proportionable sentiments and expressions (example: the bell in Venice Preserved; Hamlet's Ghost as a masterly effect). They must prepare the mind of the reader/viewer and not be mere tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the actor's speech and feeling match his visible signs of sorrow (handkerchief rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the moving of Pity, our principal Machine is the Handkerchief ... All that I would contend for, is, to keep it from being misapplied. In a Word, I would have the Actor's Tongue sympathize with his Eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional props (like a handkerchief) are permissible but must be supported by appropriate sentiment and spoken expression; do not use such devices mechanically without congruent speech and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not multiply contrivances (e.g., children) to force pity — avoid ridiculous excess
rubrics_metrics.description: A Modern Writer ... being resolved to double the Distress ... brought a Princess upon the Stage with a little Boy in one Hand and a Girl in the other. This too had a very good Effect. A third Poet ... introduced three Children, with great Success: ... a young Gentleman ... has a Tragedy by him, where the first Person that appears upon the Stage, is an afflicted Widow in her mourning Weeds, with half a Dozen fatherless Children attending her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While such incidents may move pity in good hands, they easily become ludicrous in bad hands; devices should be used with restraint and taste rather than as a formula for emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid representing murders and bloody butchery onstage
rubrics_metrics.description: Among all our Methods of moving Pity or Terror, there is none so absurd and barbarous ... than that dreadful butchering of one another, which is so very frequent upon the English Stage. To delight in seeing Men stabbed, poisoned, racked, or impaled, is certainly the Sign of a cruel Temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On-stage slaughter is indecent and exposes the theatre to ridicule; murders and executions are better transacted offstage (as in the French theatre) or related, preserving decorum and avoiding brutal spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: For delicate violent situations, execute action offstage and use heard dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Sophocles ... conveys himself by a beautiful Stratagem into his Mother's Apartment with a Resolution to kill her. But because such a Spectacle would have been too shocking to the Audience, this dreadful Resolution is executed behind the Scenes: The Mother is heard calling out to her Son for Mercy; and the Son answering her ... we find that she is slain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The offstage execution and the ensuing heard dialogue can be more affecting than an explicit onstage depiction; ancient practice shows restraint heightens emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle aids the vulgar audience but cannot substitute for good writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tailor and the Painter often contribute to the Success of a Tragedy more than the Poet. Scenes affect ordinary Minds as much as Speeches; and our Actors are very sensible, that a well-dressed Play has sometimes brought them as full Audiences, as a well-written one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that scenery and costume help draw popular audiences (the Italians call it 'Fourberia della Scena' — the knavery of the stage), but a discerning audience values thought and expression; do not let show replace substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer dignity of thought and sublimity of expression to trappings
rubrics_metrics.description: I would have our Conceptions raised by the Dignity of Thought and Sublimity of Expression, rather than by a Train of Robes or a Plume of Feathers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a positive principle: cultivate elevated ideas and noble language in the writing so that the imagination, not mere costume or machine, produces the sense of greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of artificial personal appearance: painted faces lack animation
rubrics_metrics.description: There are Women who do not let their Husbands see their Faces till they are married. ... Part of the Sex who paint. ... The Picts, tho' never so Beautiful, have dead, uninformed Countenances. The Muscles of a real Face sometimes swell with soft Passion ... But the Picts behold all things with the same Air, whether they are Joyful or Sad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artificial cosmetics can produce a fixed, lifeless aspect and deceive admirers; genuine expression (cheerfulness, good humour) enlivens features more than paint. Examine appearance closely; an oath to a 'Pict' (painted woman) is said to be void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupy idle minds with handicraft to make them useful (club/civic prescription)
rubrics_metrics.description: What I would propose should be, that we imitated those wise Nations, wherein every Man learns some Handycraft-Work. Would it not employ a Beau prettily enough, if instead of eternally playing with a Snuff-box, he spent some part of his Time in making one?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the social/political point: men disposed to dulness or vacuity should learn a mechanical art to occupy time, contribute to the public good, and avoid vain meddling in affairs for novelty's sake.
